node.label: Canada’s 1960s
node.period_rationale: Extension entry (period null). Inside 1920–2000 are early accounts (Kostash 1980, Levitt 1984), the Quiet Revolution's origins (Behiels 1985), Gélinas (1996), Martel (1997) and Owram (1996). The field's consolidation (Igartua 2006 to Milligan 2014) is post-2000.
node.date_label: Early accounts: Kostash 1980, Levitt 1984 · Behiels 1985 · Owram 1996 · Igartua 2006 · Palmer, Warren 2008–09 · Mills 2010 · Debating Dissent 2012 · coverage through 2000; mostly post-2000 extension

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. Participants' and journalists' writing on the decade began earlier; 1980 is the first selected book and 2020 the latest. Neither bounds the field.

node.description: Historical writing that treats Canada's long 1960s as a subject in its own right: the baby boom and youth revolt, the New Left and labour militancy, Quebec's Quiet Revolution and its radicalisms, rights movements, decolonization and Red Power, and the remaking of national identity. Book-length accounts began with Kostash's interview-based history of her own generation (1980) and Levitt (1984). Doug Owram's Born at the Right Time (1996) followed the baby-boom generation from suburb and school to counterculture and youth radicalism. José Igartua's The Other Quiet Revolution (2006) traced English Canada's British self-definition giving way to a civic, rights-based identity, and Dominique Clément studied its rights associations. Bryan Palmer's Canada's 1960s (2009) read the decade through the ironies of national identity, with chapters on wildcat strikes, the New Left, Quebec and the 'discovery' of the 'Indian'. Sean Mills's The Empire Within (2010) traced postcolonial thought in Montreal activism, and David Austin race, sex and security there. Campbell, Clément and Kealey's Debating Dissent (2012) and Ian Milligan's Rebel Youth (2014), on young workers and New Leftists, widened the field. Francophone historians debate continuity and rupture. Michael Behiels, E.-Martin Meunier and Jean-Philippe Warren, and Louise Bienvenue found the Quiet Revolution's roots in postwar liberalism and in Catholic Action, against its own story of a 'grande noirceur'. Warren's Une douce anarchie (2008) historicized the student revolt of 1968. It is a recent synthesis literature resting on a few reference works (Owram, Palmer, Mills, Igartua), not a school like the atlas's New Left entry.
node.scope_note: A research field defined by its subject, the long 1960s (roughly late 1950s to early 1970s), not by a method or school. It replaces the "postwar Canada" data cluster (user, 2026-10-12: "1960s is its own thing"). Distinguish the atlas's New Left entry (radical historians as a school) from histories of the New Left as a movement. The Quebec strand overlaps Quebec historiography and the Catholic Action revision in religion history; those works keep their primary placements there. Register (answers Q94): a recent synthesis literature resting on a few reference works (Owram 71 and Palmer 67 citing PhDs; Mills; Igartua), with engagement modestly falling (ratio 0.78; fixed panel 0.81), not a school. Black Canadian sixties history: Austin (2013) covers the post-2000 extension; before 2000 the only verified work is a contemporary participants' collection (Forsythe, ed., 1971), so pre-2000 scholarly coverage is a gap.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Kostash, Long Way from Home (1980); Levitt, Children of Privilege (1984); Behiels, Prelude to Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (1985); Couture, Le mythe de la modernisation du Québec (1991); Owram, Born at the Right Time (1996); Gélinas (1996, 2007); Martel, Le deuil d’un pays imaginé (1997); Meunier and Warren (2002); Bienvenue (2003); Gauvreau (2005); Igartua, The Other Quiet Revolution (2006); Clément, Canada’s Rights Revolution (2008); Warren, Une douce anarchie (2008); Palmer, Canada’s 1960s (2009); Mills, The Empire Within (2010); Kinsman and Gentile (2010); Henderson, Making the Scene (2011); Campbell, Clément and Kealey, eds., Debating Dissent (2012); Austin, Fear of a Black Nation (2013) (with Forsythe, ed., Let the Niggers Burn!, 1971, as a contemporary participants' collection); Milligan, Rebel Youth (2014); Rutherford, Canada’s Other Red Scare (2020). Comparison: Marwick, The Sixties (1998).

representative_people.name: Doug Owram
representative_people.context: Writes the first Canadian history of the baby-boom generation, from family and suburb to counterculture, youth radicalism and sexual revolution.
representative_people.works: Born at the Right Time (1996)

representative_people.name: Myrna Kostash
representative_people.context: An interview-based history of the sixties generation by a member of it (1980): a participant-observer who by her own account was on the edge of the movements, not a leader. Not a memoir.
representative_people.works: Long Way from Home (1980)

representative_people.name: José E. Igartua
representative_people.context: Argues that English Canada underwent its own "quiet revolution" as ethnic, British definitions of identity gave way to civic, rights-based ones, 1945–71; also writes on the sixties in Quebec.
representative_people.works: The Other Quiet Revolution (2006); “The Sixties in Quebec” (2012)

representative_people.name: Dominique Clément
representative_people.context: Rights associations as social movements, 1937–82; coeditor of Debating Dissent and coauthor of its introduction on time, age and myth.
representative_people.works: Canada’s Rights Revolution (2008); Debating Dissent (2012), ed. with Lara Campbell and Gregory S. Kealey

representative_people.name: Lara Campbell
representative_people.context: Coeditor of Debating Dissent and coauthor of its introduction, "Time, Age, Myth: Towards a History of the Sixties".
representative_people.works: Debating Dissent (2012), ed. with Dominique Clément and Gregory S. Kealey

representative_people.name: Bryan D. Palmer
representative_people.context: Reads the decade through the ironies of Canadian identity, with chapters on wildcat strikes, the New Left, Quebec and the "discovery" of the "Indian"; also writes on Red Power. Primary placement in working-class history.
representative_people.works: Canada’s 1960s (2009); “‘Indians of All Tribes’: The Birth of Red Power” (2012)

representative_people.name: Ian Milligan
representative_people.context: Treats young workers' wildcat militancy and the New Left as one youth revolt. The same person as the atlas's digital-history Ian Milligan (Waterloo); the citation graph mis-parses him as "Gerry".
representative_people.works: Rebel Youth (2014)

representative_people.name: Stuart Henderson
representative_people.context: Yorkville and hip Toronto; metadata only.
representative_people.works: Making the Scene (2011)

representative_people.name: Sean Mills
representative_people.context: Studies postcolonial thought in Montreal's political activism, from Black and feminist movements to labour and the FLQ; reviewed Warren's history of 1968.
representative_people.works: The Empire Within (2010)

representative_people.name: David Austin
representative_people.context: Race, sex and security in sixties Montreal: the 1968 Congress of Black Writers and the Black-led protest at Sir George Williams University (description checked). The main post-2000 study of Black Canadian sixties history in this draft; before 2000 the verified account is Forsythe's contemporary collection (1971).
representative_people.works: Fear of a Black Nation (2013)

representative_people.name: Gary Kinsman
representative_people.context: With Patrizia Gentile, the national-security campaign against gays and lesbians from the 1950s to the 1990s. Primary placement in moral regulation.
representative_people.works: The Canadian War on Queers (2010), with Patrizia Gentile

representative_people.name: Scott Rutherford
representative_people.context: Indigenous protest in the 1960s as local and transnational, confronting settler colonialism.
representative_people.works: Canada’s Other Red Scare (2020)

representative_people.name: Michael D. Behiels
representative_people.context: The Quiet Revolution's postwar intellectual origins in Cité libre liberalism and neo-nationalism, 1945–60.
representative_people.works: Prelude to Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (1985)

representative_people.name: Jean-Philippe Warren
representative_people.context: Historicizes Quebec's student revolt of 1968 and its rapid collapse; with Meunier, locates personalist Catholic roots of the Quiet Revolution.
representative_people.works: Sortir de la « grande noirceur » (2002), with E.-Martin Meunier; Une douce anarchie (2008)

representative_people.name: Louise Bienvenue
representative_people.context: Catholic Action and youth as a constructed category before the Quiet Revolution. Primary placement may be religion or Quebec historiography.
representative_people.works: Quand la jeunesse entre en scène (2003)

representative_people.name: Michael Gauvreau
representative_people.context: Traces Catholic Action's reshaping of family and gender into the 1960s. Primary placement in religion, social reform and secularization.
representative_people.works: The Catholic Origins of Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (2005)

representative_people.name: Xavier Gélinas
representative_people.context: The intellectual right in the Quiet Revolution, between left neo-nationalism and Duplessis conservatism.
representative_people.works: “La droite intellectuelle et la Révolution tranquille” (1996); La droite intellectuelle québécoise et la Révolution tranquille (2007)

representative_people.name: Marcel Martel
representative_people.context: The Quiet Revolution's effect on French Canada outside Quebec, and the Sir George Williams "riot" as student dissent. Primary placement in Quebec historiography.
representative_people.works: Le deuil d’un pays imaginé (1997); “‘Riot’ at Sir George Williams” (2012)

representative_people.name: Claude Couture
representative_people.context: Title-level: questions the modernization story running from the 1930s to the Quiet Revolution. Argument unread.
representative_people.works: Le mythe de la modernisation du Québec (1991)

representative_people.name: Arthur Marwick
representative_people.context: International comparator: the long sixties (c. 1958–74) as a cultural revolution in four Western countries. Already an atlas person.
representative_people.works: The Sixties (1998)

strands.title: The baby boom, youth and counterculture
strands.focus: The generation as subject: family, suburb, school, the teenager, the hip scene, student revolt and sexual revolution. Kostash's early account is an interview-based history by a member of the generation.

strands.title: English Canada's other Quiet Revolution and the rights revolution
strands.focus: The end of British Canada, civic national identity, rights associations, nationalism and language rights.
strands.works: Igartua (2006); Clément (2008); Champion (2010); Azzi and Hayday in Debating Dissent (2012)

strands.title: New Left, students and young workers
strands.focus: The New Left and student movements studied together with wildcat strikes and young workers' militancy.
strands.works: Palmer (2009); Lexier and McInnis in Debating Dissent (2012); Milligan (2014)

strands.title: Decolonization, race, Red Power and the security state
strands.focus: Postcolonial thought in Montreal, Black radicalism, Indigenous protest, and state surveillance of queers, women's liberation and radicals. Pre-2000 scholarly coverage of Black Canadian sixties history is a gap; Forsythe (1971) is a contemporary source, not scholarship.
strands.works: Forsythe, ed. (1971), a contemporary participants' collection; Mills (2010); Kinsman and Gentile (2010); Walker, Palmer, Hewitt and Sethna in Debating Dissent (2012); Austin (2013); Rutherford (2020)

strands.title: Quebec: continuity, rupture and 1968
strands.focus: Francophone historians debate whether the Quiet Revolution broke with a "grande noirceur" or grew from postwar liberal, neo-nationalist, right-wing and Catholic Action currents; Warren historicizes the 1968 revolt; Martel follows the break-up of French Canada.
strands.works: Behiels (1985); Couture (1991); Gélinas (1996, 2007); Martel (1997); Meunier and Warren (2002); Bienvenue (2003); Gauvreau (2005); Warren (2008); Igartua, “The Sixties in Quebec” (2012)

strands.title: The sixties as history, myth and global moment
strands.focus: Historians separate the decade from its participants' memory and myth, and set it in international and global frames.
strands.works: Marwick (1998); Dubinsky, Krull, Lord et al., eds. (2009); Campbell and Clément, introduction to Debating Dissent (2012)

relation_to_periods: The main period is 1920–2000; the selected in-period works are early accounts (1980–85) and 1990s Quebec and baby-boom studies. Recommended as an extension entry with period null.

proposed_relationships.relationship: A radical historians' school and a field about the decade
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: The atlas entry is a US school of radical historians; the Canadian field studies the New Left as a subject: Palmer's chapter "New Left Liberations", Milligan on New Leftists and young workers, Lexier on student movements in Debating Dissent. Comparison only; no checked source claims descent from the US school.

proposed_relationships.relationship: The Quiet Revolution as shared subject: continuity or rupture
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Behiels locates the Quiet Revolution's origins in postwar liberalism and neo-nationalism; Gauvreau's review describes the revisionist challenge to "the conventional ideology of the Quiet Revolution"; Mills's review follows Warren's 1968; Igartua contributes "The Sixties in Quebec". PhD context: 18 of 136 PhDs engaging this draft are at francophone universities. Target is proposed.
proposed_relationships.coordination: Duplicates qcreq_rel_08 (quebec_historiography – cdn_sixties comparison) in the quebec_historiography draft, which invited the Sixties drafter to supply stronger evidence. Keep one edge, merging that draft's Rouillard evidence with this one's.

proposed_relationships.relationship: The sixties between memory, myth and history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Hébert: "les années 68 sont devenues mythiques", built on oral tradition and memory, and Warren brings them into scholarship; Campbell and Clément title their introduction "Time, Age, Myth: Towards a History of the Sixties". Comparison: the field historicizes memory rather than adopting memory-studies method.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Decolonization thought as a subject of sixties history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Mills's subtitle and chapters ("The International Dimension of Resistance", "The Language of Liberation") study activists' use of postcolonial thought; Rutherford places Indigenous protest in a transnational frame. PhD context: 10 of 53 PhDs citing Mills also cite Fanon (lift 5.2). Comparison: anti-colonial writing is the historians' subject, not their method.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Young workers, wildcat strikes and the New Left
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Milligan treats young workers' wildcat militancy and the New Left as one youth revolt; Palmer's chapter "Wildcat Workers"; McInnis on sixties wildcat strikes in Debating Dissent. Target is proposed.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Sexual regulation and surveillance in the 1960s
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Kinsman and Gentile on national security as sexual regulation from the 1950s; Hewitt and Sethna on RCMP "sex spying" on women's liberation groups (Debating Dissent); Palmer's chapter "Scandalous Sex". Target is proposed.

proposed_relationships.relationship: The baby boom and youth as a historical category
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Owram's chapters on babies, school days and "the cult of the teenager"; Gauvreau credits Bienvenue with treating youth as a constructed category rather than an anthropological constant. Target is proposed.
proposed_relationships.coordination: Duplicates ccy_rel_03 (cdn_childhood_youth – cdn_sixties comparison) in the cdn_childhood_youth draft. Keep one edge; this version adds contents-level evidence (Owram's chapters, Gauvreau on Bienvenue).

open_questions: Period: extension (null) as drafted, or period_3 because of Owram 1996, Behiels 1985 and Martel 1997?

Primary placements for Warren, Bienvenue, Gauvreau and Martel: this entry, Quebec historiography or religion? The draft makes Warren (Une douce anarchie) and Gélinas primary here and leaves the others to their other groups.
Should Kostash (1980) be described as a participant account? Only metadata was checked.
Is "Topic field" acceptable as entry_type (the brief's term), or should it be "Research field"?

Engagement is steady-to-falling (10.0% to 9.1% of PhDs citing two or more listed works). Owram (71 PhDs) and Palmer (67) dominate; is the field better described as a few reference works than a school?
Black Canadian sixties history (Austin, Walker) is title-level only; should a Black history relation be checked before review?

question_resolutions.summary: Kept as an extension entry (period null) with period_3 roots in the date label; the field's most-cited works run from 1994 to 2010 (median 2005).

Martel keeps Quebec historiography as his primary placement (his readers engage the Sixties 69% and Quebec historiography 67%); Warren and Gélinas stay primary here and Bienvenue and Gauvreau keep their other placements.

Kostash (1980) is now described as an interview-based history by a member of the generation, a participant-observer on the edge of the movements by her own account, not a memoir or a leader's account; c60_kostash_1980 is supporting_page_checked (Lorimer copy; Atlantis interview).
entry_type changed from 'Topic field' to 'Research field' (atlas vocabulary); the scope note now says 'research field defined by its subject'.

The description and scope note now present the field as a recent synthesis literature resting on a few reference works (Owram, Palmer, Mills, Igartua), not a school, with the modest decline in engagement (ratio 0.78; panel 0.81) recorded in the scope note.

Austin (2013) is now description-checked and carries the post-2000 extension; Forsythe, ed., 1971 is added as a metadata-checked contemporary participants' collection, explicitly not scholarship; pre-2000 scholarly coverage is marked as a gap. No black – cdn_sixties edge is proposed.
